title: Conformal Prediction Under Covariate Shift
research_question: Can conformal prediction retain distribution-free marginal coverage when training and test covariate distributions differ while the conditional outcome distribution given covariates remains unchanged?
methodology: The paper develops weighted conformal prediction by replacing ordinary empirical quantiles of nonconformity scores with importance-weighted quantiles derived from the likelihood ratio between test and training covariate distributions. It formalizes a broader notion of weighted exchangeability and proves coverage guarantees, then derives a computationally simple split-conformal specialization for covariate shift. An empirical study uses the UCI Airfoil dataset over 5,000 random trials, comparing unweighted, oracle-weighted, and estimated-weight procedures; reproduction code is provided.

key_findings.finding: When the covariate likelihood ratio is known, weighted conformal prediction restores finite-sample marginal coverage under covariate shift while ordinary conformal prediction need not retain its nominal coverage.
The method is derived from a more general weighted-exchangeability framework that includes ordinary exchangeability and certain independent non-identically distributed settings as special cases.
In the Airfoil experiment at 90% nominal coverage, ordinary split conformal averaged 90.2% without shift but only 82.2% on the shifted test distribution.
Using the oracle covariate-shift weights raised average coverage on the shifted Airfoil test distribution to 90.8%.
Importance weighting increases coverage variability because highly uneven weights reduce the effective calibration sample size.

The needed density ratio can be estimated from unlabeled test covariates by training a classifier to distinguish training from test inputs, although correctness then depends on estimation quality rather than the exact oracle-weight theorem.

General weighted conformal quantiles can be combinatorially difficult, but the covariate-shift structure yields a computationally tractable specialization comparable in complexity to ordinary conformal prediction.

limitations: The covariate-shift result assumes that the conditional distribution of the response given covariates remains unchanged between training and test populations.
Exact finite-sample validity in the principal covariate-shift result relies on knowing the likelihood ratio between test and training covariate distributions.
When the likelihood ratio is estimated, practical validity depends on the accuracy and stability of density-ratio estimation.
Highly variable importance weights reduce effective sample size and make intervals and empirical coverage more variable.
The main empirical demonstration uses one relatively small, five-dimensional Airfoil dataset with synthetically induced exponential tilting.
The paper provides marginal rather than exact pointwise conditional coverage; exact distribution-free conditional coverage is discussed as generally unattainable without uninformative intervals.
The fully general weighted-exchangeability construction can be computationally difficult.
raw_claims: Ordinary conformal validity follows from exchangeability and can fail when the test covariate distribution changes.
The weighted method assigns calibration observations influence according to their relevance to the test covariate distribution.
Covariate-shift weights are proportional to the density ratio between test and training covariate distributions.
The covariate-shift setting keeps the conditional response distribution given the covariates fixed.
Weighted conformal prediction achieves the required marginal coverage when the shift weights are known.
The Airfoil experiment used 5,000 random trials and a nominal coverage target of 90%.
Ordinary split conformal substantially undercovered the synthetically shifted Airfoil population.
Oracle weighting brought the shifted-population coverage back close to the target.
Uneven importance weights effectively reduce the usable calibration sample size.
A probabilistic classifier can estimate the training-to-test density ratio using unlabeled test covariates.
The authors released R code for the Airfoil simulations.
Weighted conformal prediction extends beyond covariate shift to other weighted-exchangeable settings.
